# 21 · How to tell whether an agent team is worth the extra work

## Start here

This lesson needs only the distinction between one assistant and several coordinated workers. If you want a refresher, read [delegation](19.md) and [coordination](20.md). You do not need to launch agents to understand the comparison.

For an SDET, the question resembles evaluating a new testing tool: does it find important problems more reliably, and what does it cost to use and maintain? A busy screen with several agents working is not a quality metric. Start with the outcome you need, then measure the work that produced it.

## The idea in plain language

A **baseline** is the simpler approach you compare against. Here it might be one assistant following a good checklist. A **candidate** is the alternative you are considering, such as a coordinator with two reviewers. A **paired comparison** gives both approaches the same cases so you can inspect where their outcomes differ.

Keep evidence access and judging rules the same. If the team receives a missing requirement that the baseline never saw, you have changed both the architecture and the information. That extra difference is a **confounder**: a reason you cannot confidently attribute the improvement to teamwork alone.

Measure quality, important failures, time, and resource use separately. **Elapsed time** is how long the learner or user waits. **Total work** includes every worker and the parent's integration. Parallel workers can finish sooner while consuming more total effort. Model tokens, currency, and human review minutes are different units; do not add them into a number without explaining a meaningful conversion.

Inspect regressions: cases the candidate handles worse than the baseline. An improved average may coexist with a serious new mistake. Also inspect coordination problems even when the final answer happens to be acceptable. A stale result accepted during a small test is a warning about the process.

This comparison is unnecessary when you are simply reading about agents. It becomes valuable before investing in a more complex assistant workflow or claiming that a team is better. A small teaching sample can reveal a defect; it cannot estimate performance on every future workload.

## A small example

Here are invented outcomes for a test-plan reviewer. “Pass” means a human checked the same requirement rubric for both approaches.

| Case | One assistant | Team | One-assistant calls | All team calls |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Q1 | Pass | Pass | 1 | 3 |
| Q2 | Fail | Pass | 1 | 4 |
| Q3 | Pass | Fail | 1 | 3 |
| Q4 | Fail | Pass | 1 | 4 |

The baseline passes 2/4; the team passes 3/4. The team improves Q2 and Q4 but regresses Q3, while calls rise from 4 to 14. Suppose Q3's team output claims a test ran when it did not. That matters even though the total pass count rose.

These numbers are supplied teaching data, not measured model results. They demonstrate how to interpret a comparison. Whether extra calls are worth it depends on the value of the improvements and the severity of the regression.

## Try it with Codex or Claude Code

1. Open either assistant. No repository is needed; [the assistant quickstart](../../docs/ASSISTANT-QUICKSTART.md) explains project access if you want it.
2. Paste this prompt with all the comparison data:

```text
Help me interpret synthetic results, without running agents or editing files.
Both systems received identical requirements and the same reviewed pass/fail rubric.
Case | single outcome | team outcome | single calls | all team calls
Q1 | pass | pass | 1 | 3
Q2 | fail | pass | 1 | 4
Q3 | pass | fail | 1 | 3
Q4 | fail | pass | 1 | 4
Q3 team failure: claimed a test had run without execution evidence.
Calculate pass counts and call totals. List improvements and regressions.
Explain what these four cases do and do not show. Suggest one next comparison,
without claiming the team is ready to release. Do not invent time or cost data.
Use plain language and label this supplied-data analysis, not a live benchmark.
```

3. Recount the four rows yourself. You should be able to reproduce the arithmetic without trusting an assistant-generated percentage.
4. Ask: “What would make a future comparison unfair?” Check that it mentions changed inputs, judging rules, or hidden extra resources.
5. Stop after you can explain why the better aggregate does not settle the decision. You do not need to build an evaluation dashboard.

## What you should see

The answer should identify two improvements, one regression, and 4 versus 14 calls. It should keep the unsupported execution claim visible. It must not invent currency costs, measured latency, statistical significance, or an actual worker run.

A useful next experiment changes one clear thing or examines the failing case. Automatically adding a fourth reviewer is a proposed design change, not evidence that the problem is solved.

## If it goes wrong

If it declares “50% better” and stops, ask it to show the case-level losses and the denominator behind that statement. If it counts only worker calls, clarify whether parent calls are included. If workers agree, ask whether they checked distinct evidence or repeated the same source. If both systems fail, inspect the requirements and rubric before assuming that more agents will help.

## Go deeper

Read **Effective evaluation of agents** in Anthropic's [How we built our multi-agent research system](https://www.anthropic.com/research/multi-agent-research-system). Stop before **Production reliability and engineering challenges**. Prerequisite: understand baseline, rubric, and worker. It is public reading, with no product account required. Treat the company's measurements as results for its described system, not predictions for yours. Checked 21 October 2026.

The [evaluation-versus-demo article](../articles/evaluation-vs-demo.md) and [worker practicum](../labs/13-coding-and-workers.md) offer related reading and optional execution. The practicum explicitly distinguishes scripted worker processes from actual assistant workers.

## Optional practice

Ask your tutor for a new three-case comparison. Identify the improved cases, regressions, and one missing measurement before requesting feedback.
